presentingComplaint: Central crushing chest pain for 3 hours with breathlessness and sweating
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 13) under hepatology follow-up, with prior variceal banding and grade 1 ascites. Also hypertensive and type 2 diabetic. For the last month he had described exertional chest tightness while climbing stairs that eased on rest, initially attributed to deconditioning and anaemia of chronic liver disease. Today, while at rest, he developed severe retrosternal pressure radiating to the left arm and jaw, associated with diaphoresis, nausea and breathlessness, unrelieved after 20 minutes. He denies haematemesis, melaena, fever or preceding vomiting. No recent variceal bleed or paracentesis. He is a lifelong smoker (40 pack-years) and stopped alcohol 8 months ago. The overlap of his baseline hyperdynamic cirrhotic circulation, low-grade breathlessness and mild ankle oedema had previously masked cardiac symptoms.
examination: Anxious, diaphoretic, in pain but alert (GCS 15). Peripherally warm with bounding pulses reflecting hyperdynamic cirrhotic circulation. Mild scleral icterus and a few spider naevi. JVP not raised; heart sounds normal with no new murmur; chest with fine bibasal crackles. Abdomen soft with mild shifting dullness (grade 1 ascites), no tenderness, spleen tip palpable. No asterixis, oriented, no focal neurology. No calf swelling.
imaging: ECG: sinus tachycardia with 1.5-2 mm horizontal ST depression and T-wave inversion in leads V4-V6, II, III, aVF; no ST elevation. Portable chest X-ray: mild upper-lobe vascular redistribution, no consolidation or pneumothorax. Bedside echo: regional hypokinesia of the inferolateral wall, LVEF ~45%, no pericardial effusion, normal aortic root.
microbiology: Not applicable; no infective focus. Blood cultures not indicated.
finalDiagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI) in a patient with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B), with coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia complicating antithrombotic therapy
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Non-ST-Segment Elevation Acute Coronary Syndrome
ESC — Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes — 2023
stewardship: Non-infective presentation: no antimicrobial therapy indicated; antimicrobial stewardship tier is null. Management stewardship centres on antithrombotic and anti-ischaemic therapy balanced against cirrhotic coagulopathy. Give aspirin loading and anti-ischaemic therapy (nitrate, beta-blocker as BP/HR allow), high-intensity statin used cautiously with LFT monitoring in Child-Pugh B, and risk-stratify (GRACE) for early invasive coronary angiography. Because thrombocytopenia (78) and elevated INR reflect hepatic synthetic dysfunction rather than true anticoagulation, DAPT and anticoagulation decisions must be individualised with cardiology-hepatology input, favouring radial access, weight/renal-adjusted anticoagulation, and shortened DAPT duration to limit variceal/GI bleeding risk. Avoid empirical antibiotics.
contraindications: Full-dose thrombolysis / aggressive anticoagulation without weighing variceal and coagulopathic bleeding risk
Standard-duration potent dual antiplatelet therapy (e.g., ticagrelor/prasugrel) without bleeding-risk assessment given thrombocytopenia and cirrhosis
Nephrotoxic contrast load without hydration in a patient prone to hepatorenal physiology
NSAIDs for chest pain in cirrhosis with ascites
edgeCases: Cirrhotic hyperdynamic circulation and baseline breathlessness can mask or mimic anginal symptoms and delay presentation
Elevated INR and thrombocytopenia here reflect liver disease, not therapeutic anticoagulation, and do not protect against coronary thrombosis
Troponin may be mildly elevated in stable cirrhosis; the dynamic rise plus ischaemic ECG and regional wall-motion abnormality confirms ACS
Statin hepatotoxicity fears often lead to inappropriate under-treatment in compensated cirrhosis
expectedMaiK: Dynamic troponin rise with ischaemic ST depression/T inversion and regional wall-motion abnormality confirms NSTEMI; cirrhosis modifies antithrombotic strategy but not the diagnosis
